summary.text: The prime number theorem describes how primes are spread among the positive integers, making precise the idea that primes become less common as numbers get larger.
For large N, the chance that a random integer up to N is prime is very close to 1 / log(N).
It was proved independently in 1896 by Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin, using ideas introduced by Bernhard Riemann.

paragraphs.heading: How primes thin out
paragraphs.text: The prime number theorem describes how prime numbers are spread out among the positive integers. Most people sense that primes get rarer as numbers get bigger; the theorem pins down exactly how fast that happens. It says that π(N) ~ N/log(N). Here π(N) is the prime-counting function, which counts how many primes are no bigger than N, and log(N) stands for the natural logarithm of N.

paragraphs.heading: What it means in practice
paragraphs.text: For large N, an integer picked at random up to N is prime with probability very close to 1 / log(N). Put another way, among the first N integers the average gap between neighbouring primes is about log(N). So, for large enough sizes, doubling the number of digits roughly halves the chance of landing on a prime. Among integers of up to 1000 digits, roughly one in 2300 is prime, while among those of up to 2000 digits it is roughly one in 4600.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the squiggle
paragraphs.text: The symbol ~ needs care. It says nothing about whether the difference between π(x) and x / log x settles down as x grows. Instead it says the relative error of the approximation goes to 0 as x grows without bound. A similar estimate works for the primes themselves: the 2×10¹⁷th prime is 8512677386048191063, while the estimate (2×10¹⁷)log(2×10¹⁷) comes to about 7967418752291744388. That is off by roughly 6.4% in relative terms.

paragraphs.heading: Early guesses
paragraphs.text: The law was guessed long before it was proved. Adrien-Marie Legendre, drawing on prime tables by Anton Felkel and Jurij Vega, guessed in 1797 or 1798 that π(a) is close to a / (A log a + B) for some constants A and B, and in 1808 he proposed A = 1 and B = −1.08366. Carl Friedrich Gauss recalled in 1849 that he had thought about the same question at 15 or 16. In 1838 Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet offered the logarithmic integral li(x) as his approximation. Both formulas point to the same law, but Dirichlet's is much better if you compare differences rather than ratios.

paragraphs.heading: Chebyshev and Riemann
paragraphs.text: The Russian mathematician Pafnuty Chebyshev tried, in two papers of 1848 and 1850, to prove the law. He showed that if the ratio of π(x) to x / log(x) has a limit at all, it must equal one, and that for all large enough x the ratio stays between 0.92129 and 1.10555. That was enough for him to prove Bertrand's postulate: for any integer n ≥ 2 there is a prime between n and 2n. Then in 1859 Bernhard Riemann wrote his only paper on the subject, tying the spread of primes to the zeros of the zeta function and bringing complex analysis to bear on π(x).

paragraphs.heading: The proofs
paragraphs.text: Building on Riemann's ideas, Jacques Hadamard and Charles Jean de la Vallée Poussin each proved the theorem independently in 1896. Both proofs used complex analysis, and a main step was showing that the zeta function ζ(s) is nonzero at every point s = 1 + it with t > 0. Those original proofs are long and elaborate. Other proofs followed, including the "elementary" ones of Atle Selberg and Paul Erdős in 1949, and a short proof by the American mathematician Donald J. Newman in 1980 that is arguably the simplest known.
